content: Epinephrine aerosol is an adrenergic, sympathomimetic, and bronchodilator agent approved by the FDA for the temporary relief of shortness of breath, chest tightness, and wheezing caused by bronchial asthma. It works by reducing spasms in the bronchial muscles, thereby easing breathing in asthma patients. Common adverse reactions include nausea, vomiting, dizziness, headache, anxiety, sweating, and palpitations. For adults, the FDA-approved indication is for the symptomatic control of bronchial asthma. Off-label use in adults is not well-documented, and there is limited information regarding guideline-supported or non-guideline-supported off-label use. For pediatric patients, there is limited information regarding FDA-approved indications and dosage. Similarly, off-label use in pediatric patients, whether guideline-supported or not, is not well-documented. Epinephrine aerosol should not be used unless a diagnosis of asthma has been made by a physician. It is contraindicated in individuals with heart disease, high blood pressure, thyroid disease, diabetes, or difficulty urinating due to prostate enlargement unless directed by a physician. It should not be used by individuals who have been hospitalized for asthma or are taking prescription asthma medications unless directed by a physician. Excessive use may cause nervousness, rapid heartbeat, and potentially adverse effects on the heart. If symptoms are not relieved within 20 minutes or worsen, medical assistance should be sought immediately. The product is intended for oral inhalation only and should not be used more frequently or at higher doses than recommended unless directed by a physician. Pregnant or nursing individuals should consult a healthcare professional before use. The product should be kept out of reach of children, and in case of accidental overdose, professional assistance or a poison control center should be contacted immediately. Adverse reactions reported during clinical trials include nausea, vomiting, dizziness, headache, anxiety, sweating, and palpitations. Postmarketing experience data is limited. Epinephrine aerosol should not be used concurrently with prescription drugs for high blood pressure or depression without consulting a physician. There is no FDA guidance on its use in specific populations, including pregnant or nursing women, pediatric or geriatric patients, or individuals with renal or hepatic impairment. Additionally, there is no established guidance on its use in immunocompromised patients, specific gender or racial populations, or individuals of reproductive potential. The product is supplied in a shatterproof aluminum canister with a specially designed valve and is intended for use with the MEDIHALER-EPI oral adapter. The canister delivers a consistent dose with each use, and the adapter should be cleaned daily with soap and hot water. The product should be stored at controlled room temperature (15°C to 30°C or 59°F to 86°F) and away from heat or temperatures above 120°F, as this may cause the canister to burst. For adults and children aged 4 years and older, the recommended dosage is one inhalation, followed by at least one minute before a second inhalation if needed. The product should not be used again for at least three hours. Children under 4 years of age should consult a physician before use. The use of this product by children should be supervised by an adult. Before each use, the dust cap should be removed, and the oral adapter should be inspected for foreign objects. The canister should be shaken well. To administer the medication, the user should exhale fully, place the mouthpiece into the mouth aimed at the back of the throat, and press the canister firmly while inhaling deeply. The breath should be held as long as possible before exhaling slowly. The dust cap should be replaced after each use. There is no established interaction between alcohol and epinephrine aerosol, but patients should consult their doctor regarding the effects of alcohol with this medication. Information regarding brand names, look-alike drug names, pharmacology, pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, and nonclinical toxicology is limited in the drug label.
